You express wishes and good wishes at B2 level: ojalá + present / imperfect / pluperfect subjunctive (a possible, unlikely or impossible wish), que + subjunctive for good wishes (¡Que te mejores!, ¡Que aproveche!), a ver si + indicative, ¡quién + imperfect subjunctive! (¡Quién pudiera!) and verbs of wishing (espero que, me encantaría que).
I wish I could! / Lucky you!
If only they take the cast off in time.
If only it were three weeks and not six.
Hopefully you’ll be able to sign by April.
To choose the subjunctive tense after “ojalá” according to how possible the wish is: present (possible), imperfect (unlikely), pluperfect (impossible, in the past).
To make good wishes with “que + present subjunctive”: ¡Que te mejores!, ¡Que aproveche!, ¡Que tengas suerte!
To express colloquial hopes with “a ver si + indicative”: A ver si llueve.
To express impossible wishes or friendly envy with “¡Quién + imperfect subjunctive!”: ¡Quién pudiera!
To use verbs of wishing with the subjunctive and the sequence of tenses: espero que vengas, me encantaría que vinieras.
Tuesday, 3 March, the emergency department of a hospital in Bucharest. Ecaterina slipped on the ice outside the post office. Ana came at once. The doctor has just looked at the X-ray.
You’ve broken your right wrist, madam. Six weeks in plaster.
Six weeks? If only it were three! On 23 April I have to sign books in Madrid.
If only they take the cast off in time. Is it possible, doctor?
If all goes well, yes. Hopefully we can take it off by mid-April.
I wish I were twenty! At that age bones heal on their own.
And at that age people don’t go out in heels when there’s ice, either.
Well, I was going to the post office to send a letter. I wish I hadn’t gone out today.
Don’t say that. Now the only thing that matters is that you heal properly.
Exactly. Rest, don’t do anything silly and don’t sign anything with your right hand.
Then I’ll learn to sign with my left. Readers, beware!
“ojalá le quiten” = if only they take it off
“a mediados de” = by the middle of
“ojalá no hubiera salido” = I wish I hadn’t gone out
“que se preparen” = let them get ready
The stress falls on the last syllable: o-ja-LÁ. The “j” is aspirated, like a strong “h”. The word comes from Arabic (“if God wills”).
Good wishes start with an unstressed “que” and rise on the verb: [ke-te-me-HO-res] ↗. Don’t confuse it with “¿Qué?” (with an accent), which is a question.
“ll” and “y” are pronounced the same in most of Spain: es-ka-YO-la. In Argentina they sound like the “s” in English “measure”: es-ka-ZHO-la.
Ojalá me quiten la escayola a tiempo.
“Ojalá” can be followed by “que”, but it isn’t obligatory: «Ojalá (que) llegue a tiempo». It is NEVER used with the indicative: «Ojalá llega» ✗.
These wishes are really a clause with an implied “espero que”: «(Espero) que te mejores». That’s why they take the subjunctive.
Hopefully we’ll see each other soon.
You’re going to Seville in April? I wish I could!
“A ver si” is followed by the INDICATIVE, even though it expresses a hope: «A ver si llueve» ✓, «A ver si llueva» ✗.

The rule from chapter 85 still applies: main verb in the present → present subjunctive; main verb in the conditional or past → imperfect subjunctive.

The messages Ecaterina received in the club’s group chat on the evening of the accident. Notice the good wishes.
Marta: “Get well very soon! I wish I were there to help you. I’m sending you a careful hug, so as not to hurt you.”
Andrei: “Ecaterina, what a fright! Hopefully the doctor is wrong and it’s only four weeks. Begoña says get well soon, and Begoña doesn’t wish anyone anything.”
Costel: “I wish I’d been outside the post office to catch you. Tomorrow I’m bringing you soup. Mrs Florica is already cooking.”
Lola: “Here the lamp is still on, waiting for you. Rest well! And don’t you dare sign anything until April, we want you in one piece.”
Que tenga cuidado con el hielo
Que no firme nada hasta abril

3 March dawned icy in Bucharest. It had rained in the night and then the temperature had suddenly dropped, so the pavements had turned into skating rinks. Ecaterina didn’t notice. She left home at nine, in her good coat and her low-heeled boots, with a letter for Pilar in her hand, the first she had written to Seville. She wanted to post it, as in the old days, even though Ana had told her a thousand times that an email arrived sooner.

Outside the post office, three metres from the door, she stepped on an invisible patch of ice. The last thing she remembered was the letter flying through the air, like a white bird, and then the ground, very hard and very cold. She tried to break her fall with her right hand. She heard a dry crack, like a branch snapping. A gentleman coming out of the post office helped her onto a bench, picked the letter up off the ground and gave it back to her, a little wet. Ecaterina thanked him and, before anything else, asked him to put it in the postbox.

Then she called Ana. She didn’t tell her she had fallen; she told her she thought she had broken something and that, if it wasn’t too much trouble, perhaps she could come over. Ana arrived in fifteen minutes, by taxi, with her coat over her pyjamas. She took her straight to the emergency department. There they waited two hours, in a room full of people with broken arms, legs and noses, because that morning half of Bucharest had fallen on the same patch of ice.

In the waiting room, an elderly gentleman with a bandaged nose sat down next to her. He turned out to be a retired Latin teacher who had fallen on the same corner. When he found out Ecaterina was a translator, he forgot about his nose and spent an hour talking to her about Cicero. Ecaterina asked him whether it hurt. He said yes, terribly, but that nobody had listened to him talk about Cicero for twenty years, and he wished more interesting people would fall on that corner. Ana had to go out into the corridor to laugh.

The doctor who saw her was young, with dark rings under his eyes and a good sense of humour. He looked at the X-ray, looked at Ecaterina and told her she had broken her right wrist, a clean fracture, with no complications. Six weeks in plaster. Ecaterina did the sum aloud: six weeks from 3 March was 14 April. That would leave nine days before the Madrid launch. She told the doctor she wished it were three weeks. The doctor replied that he wished he were on holiday, and neither of them was going to be lucky.

He explained that if all went well they could take the cast off in mid-April, but that afterwards she would need a few weeks of physiotherapy before she could write normally. Ecaterina asked whether she would be able to sign books. The doctor looked at her curiously and asked how many. Ecaterina said she didn’t know, perhaps a hundred, perhaps two hundred. The doctor whistled and told her that, in that case, he advised her to start learning to sign with her left hand. Ecaterina replied that that was exactly what she intended to do.

When they left the hospital, her arm in a sling and the white cast up to her elbow, Ecaterina asked Ana not to tell anyone yet. Ana promised she wouldn’t. Half an hour later, Ana had told Mihai, Mihai had told Costel, Costel had told Mrs Florica, and Mrs Florica was already peeling onions for a soup. By the evening, the club’s group chat was full of messages, and Ecaterina had to read them all with her left hand, very slowly, because she wasn’t used to scrolling with it.

That night, when everyone had gone, it hurt a great deal. She stayed awake in her armchair, her arm raised on a cushion, as the doctor had told her. She thought of her mother, of the phone call in March 1987, no, in the autumn, she corrected herself, and realised that memories slip on the ice too. She thought she wished her mother had seen the book. She thought she wished Andrés could see her now, with the cast, because he would have laughed at her. And she fell asleep thinking that both things were impossible and that, even so, it was lovely to wish for them.

Marta wrote that she wished she were there to help her. Andrei said hopefully the doctor was wrong and it was only four weeks, and added that Begoña wished her a speedy recovery, which, according to him, he had never heard her wish anyone. Costel lamented not having been outside the post office to catch her. Lola told her the lamp was still on, waiting for her, and asked her not to dare sign anything until April. Ecaterina answered them all with a single sentence, written with her left hand: “Thank you. I’m in one piece. More or less.”

The next day, Ecaterina’s home became an operations centre. Mrs Florica arrived with the soup and decided to move in for a week, without asking. Costel fitted a phone stand on the living-room table, so she could read without holding it. Señor Dan, with his usual table, designed a wooden lectern for the pages of the Romanian translation, at an angle calculated to the degree. Ecaterina said she felt like a queen with four ministers and no hands.

Grandpa Gheorghe called from the village as soon as he heard. He told her that he, at ninety-six, had never fallen on the ice, because he always held his stick in front of him, like a blind man, to feel the ground. Ecaterina confessed that she had a stick too, but that morning she had been carrying it over her arm, because she thought it looked more elegant. Grandpa was silent, and then told her very seriously that elegance was all very well, but she should have listened to her stick.

Rosa Elena arrived in the afternoon with a box of felt-tip pens. She asked permission to decorate the cast and, without waiting for an answer, started drawing. In half an hour the white cast had turned into a motorway with seven lorries, a bridge, a green lamp and a sun wearing glasses. Then she made everyone who came to the house sign the space that was left. Costel signed with a dedication in Spanish: “Get well soon, we need you for the C1.” Señor Dan signed with his full name and the date.

Ecaterina started practising her signature with her left hand that very night. She sat at the kitchen table with one of Rosa Elena’s exercise books and wrote her name a hundred times. The first ones looked like the signatures of a four-year-old with a fever. The last ones, of a six-year-old without one. She told Ana, laughing, that she wished she were ambidextrous, and that if Andrés saw her signing like that, he’d say he wouldn’t let her write a shopping list with that handwriting.

In Madrid, the news worried people more than they let on. Marta called Inés to ask whether the launch date should be changed. Inés told her no way: if Ecaterina couldn’t sign, Marta would sign, or they’d use a stamp, or readers would take the book home unsigned and be just as happy. But 23 April was not to be touched. Marta told Ecaterina on the phone. Ecaterina said she hoped Inés was right, but she had no intention of launching her first book with a stamp.

Andrei, meanwhile, was living his first month under contract. Begoña had sent him to photograph a demonstration in the Puerta del Sol, a concert at the Teatro Real and a football team’s arrival at the airport, all in the same week. He came home in the small hours, his feet destroyed. Marta left his dinner in the oven, with a note on top: “Enjoy your meal. And get some sleep, you’re up early tomorrow.” Andrei kept them all in a box. He said one day he would hold an exhibition of Marta’s notes.

He had also kept his promise: the first portrait he took under contract was of Faustino. He photographed him at his stall one Sunday morning, in his red beret, with the framed five-hundred-peseta note behind him and a book by Neruda in his hands. Faustino posed very seriously, like a general. When he saw the printed photo, he said it was flattering, but not too flattering, which was exactly what he wanted, because a bookseller who looks too handsome in a photo doesn’t inspire confidence. He hung it in his stall the next day.

One Saturday in mid-March, Begoña called him into her office. She told him she had seen a photo of Ecaterina’s cast on Lucas’s phone, with Rosa Elena’s lorries, and wanted to know who that lady with so many friends was. Andrei explained. Begoña listened in silence and then said, without looking at him: “Tell her to get well. And that on 23 April I want a photo of her signing, with whichever hand. Hopefully the good one.” Andrei didn’t know whether that was a wish or an order. With Begoña you never knew.

Costel, for his part, had started preparing for the C1, and had realised straight away that it was another world. The texts were longer, the recordings faster and the questions trickier. The Thursdays in the cab carried on, but now with Ecaterina joining by video call from her armchair, with her cast propped on a cushion. She corrected their pronunciation mercilessly. One day Señor Dan told her he wished she would break the other wrist, so she would stop correcting them. Ecaterina replied that if that happened, she would correct them with her feet.

Mrs Florica kept her word and stayed a whole week at Ecaterina’s. She cooked for her, brushed her hair, did up the buttons on her coat and read her the Romanian newspaper aloud every morning, although Ecaterina could read it perfectly well herself. On the fourth day, Mrs Florica confessed that her husband had asked her to come home, because he had been living on bread and cheese for three days. Ecaterina told her to go, it was fine. Mrs Florica replied that her husband could wait a bit longer; he had been waiting for her for forty years and hadn’t died.

On Sunday a short man in a cap with a bag of bread appeared at Ecaterina’s door. It was Mrs Florica’s husband, who had come to fetch her in person. Nobody had ever seen him. He took off his cap, greeted Ecaterina very politely, wished her a speedy recovery and told his wife, in a low voice, that he wished she would come home that same day, because the cheese had run out. Mrs Florica sighed, gathered her things and left with him. At the door she turned round and said to Ecaterina: “Forty years, you see? And he still can’t fry an egg.”

At the end of the week, Pilar’s reply to the wet letter arrived in Bucharest. It was a real letter, handwritten, on the Seville hospital’s headed paper. Pilar told her she had read it in the courtyard with the orange trees, the one she had promised to show her, and that she had had to dry two words with a hairdryer because the Bucharest rain had blurred them. She also said she hoped she would get better soon, and that if she couldn’t sign in Seville, she would hold her hand. Ecaterina read the letter three times. The third time, she cried a little, with her left hand over her eyes.

Marta called her after reading Pilar’s letter, which Ecaterina had photographed for her. She said she had an idea in case the wrist wasn’t ready: at the Madrid launch, Ecaterina would read aloud the chapter about 23 February, and Marta would sign the books for her, writing under each signature “on behalf of the author”. Ecaterina laughed and told her no way, if anyone was going to sign her book badly, it would be herself. But she thanked her for the idea. And she told her that, in any case, she would love them to read the last chapter together.

At the end of March, Inés sent her a large envelope by courier. Inside was the printed cover, on the final paper, exactly as it would appear on the book: the empty drawer, the worn wood, the rectangular mark left by the envelope. Above it, the title, in green letters: “La lámpara encendida”. Below, in smaller letters: “Madrid, 1977 – Bucharest, 1987”. And on the flap, as the art director had demanded, a line: “Cover photograph: Andrei”. Ecaterina took a photo of it with her left hand, trembling, and sent it to Andrei without writing anything.

Lola received the same photo half an hour later, and that same afternoon she changed the sign in the window. She took down the cover printed on a sheet of paper and put up the real cover in its place, which Inés had also sent her, in a wooden frame Faustino had lent her. Underneath she wrote in chalk: “23 April. The author will be here. With both hands, hopefully.” Customers began leaving notes in the notebook wishing Ecaterina a speedy recovery. A little girl drew a wrist with a plaster on it.

Andrei received it on the metro, between Sol and Antón Martín. He stared at it for so long that he missed his stop. He got off at Atocha, went up to the street and called his father. He told him his name was going to be in a book. His father asked on which page. Andrei told him it was on the flap. His father was quiet for a moment and asked whether the flap was the part that folded inwards. Andrei said yes. His father said: “Well, then let it fold properly.” Andrei didn’t know whether he was laughing or being serious. Probably both.

On 31 March, Ecaterina went back to the hospital for a check-up. The young doctor with the rings under his eyes looked at the new X-ray, scratched his head and told her the bone was knitting faster than normal for her age. Ecaterina asked him what that meant exactly. The doctor told her that if it carried on like this, perhaps they could take the cast off on 10 April, four days earlier than planned. “Let it be true!” said Ecaterina. The doctor replied that he wasn’t promising anything, but hopefully the wrist would behave as well as its owner.

When Rosa Elena heard, she took the kitchen calendar and crossed out in red felt-tip all the days that had passed since the accident. Then she drew a huge circle around 10 April and two around the 23rd. From then on, every morning before breakfast, she crossed out another day and announced aloud how many were left, in Romanian and in Spanish. Ana said it was the most motivating calendar in Bucharest. Ecaterina said it was the most stressful.

As they left, Ana asked her whether she wanted to go straight home. Ecaterina said no. She asked her to take her to the post office, the same one outside which she had fallen a month earlier. There, with her left hand, she posted a letter to Pilar, the second one. This time the pavement was dry. Ana asked her what it said. Ecaterina answered that it was just one sentence: “Let’s hope we see each other in Seville with both hands.” Then she stood looking at the postbox for a moment, as if she expected it to answer.

That evening the club gathered in her living room to celebrate the good news. Mrs Florica brought a cake with a sugar doll on top, which nobody understood until she explained it was a play on words, because “muñeca” in Spanish meant something else as well. Costel proposed a toast to fast-healing bones. Rosa Elena added one more lorry to the cast, the eighth, with the words “10 April” written on the trailer. Ecaterina raised her glass with her left hand and said, in Spanish, so that everyone would understand: “May April come soon. And may it find me with both hands.”
